subtype: Approach: ignore the letters until the first EMI is overdue [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Uday, and when I graduated the bank sent messages about my loan. I saw the notifications on the phone and swiped them away. The amount was so large that reading the letters felt like looking down from a great height. I told myself the grace period was long and I had time. Sabina asked once if I had checked the dates and I said, "It's fine." Then a notice arrived with the word "overdue" on it. The first instalment had been missed by nine days. There was a late fee, and I later learned my record had a mark that might affect the next loan I ever wanted. Avoiding the letters had not made the problem smaller. It had made it much bigger.

qa.q: By how many days was the first instalment missed?
qa.a: The first instalment had been missed by nine days.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when swiping the bank messages away?
qa.a: Uday felt frightened by the size of the loan, so reading the letters felt like looking down from a great height.

qa.q: What could Uday do right now, and why?
qa.a: Uday could open the letters, call the bank and ask what can be done about the overdue instalment, because facing it early stops further trouble.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Uday's answer that it is fine?
qa.a: Sabina probably felt worried but unsure how to push further, since Uday brushed off the question.

grounding: Anxious about the loan's size a graduate ignores bank messages in the grace period, misses the first instalment and pays a fee and a mark on the record.

subtype: Approach: ignore the letters until the first EMI is overdue [Pitfall]
passage:
Supervisor's note, 11 September. Hafsa, customer support team.
Vijay has been jumpy at his desk this week, turning his phone face down whenever it buzzed. Today he stayed back and showed me why: a message from his bank saying his first education-loan EMI, due on 5 September, is overdue, with a ₹750 late fee added and a line about reporting to the credit bureau.
He told me the moratorium ended in August. He had seen bank messages all summer and not opened one. 'Every time I thought about six lakh, I felt sick, so I just didn't look.'
I sat with him while he opened all nine messages. Most were reminders; two had the EMI date and amount. He called the bank's helpline from the meeting room and paid the overdue EMI and the fee from his salary.
I have given him the name of the employee assistance counsellor and will check in next week.

qa.q: Why did Vijay avoid opening the bank messages?
qa.a: He felt anxious and sick at the thought of six lakh, so not looking felt easier than facing it.

qa.q: What could Vijay have done during the summer instead?
qa.a: Opened each message when it came, noted the EMI date and amount, and asked the bank or a trusted adult for help if it felt overwhelming.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Hafsa as supervisor?
qa.a: Hafsa notices Vijay's jumpiness, stays with him through the messages and points him to the counsellor instead of judging.

grounding: Shows a graduate avoiding bank messages through the moratorium out of anxiety, so the first EMI is missed, a late fee is added and the credit record is at risk.

subtype: Approach: ignore the letters until the first EMI is overdue [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday night. Vidya, this is the entry you don't want to write.
The bank called today. Not a message, an actual person. My first EMI was due on the 7th. I didn't pay it because I didn't know it was due, because I haven't opened a single bank message since March. I saw 'education loan' in the preview and swiped them away. Every one.
Late fee: ₹600. And the woman on the phone said a missed payment 'may reflect on your credit history'. I didn't even know what that meant. Zeenat explained it after, while I sat on the floor.
The stupid thing is, the EMI is ₹6,900. I have that. I've had it since June.
Zeenat made me open all of them tonight, one by one, sitting right next to me. Paid the EMI and the fee online at 11 p.m. Set a reminder for the 5th of every month. Tomorrow I'm calling the branch to ask what can be done about the record.

qa.q: What does Vidya sitting on the floor suggest?
qa.a: Vidya feels overwhelmed and ashamed, seeing that avoidance turned an affordable EMI into a late fee and a mark on the record.

qa.q: What small step would stop this happening again?
qa.a: The monthly reminder helps; opening bank messages the day they arrive, even briefly, would keep dates from slipping past.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to sit through this with Vidya?
qa.a: Zeenat stays calm and practical, explaining credit history and sitting close, probably worried but glad to help.

grounding: Shows a graduate who swiped away bank messages out of anxiety, missed the first EMI and got a late fee and a credit-record warning.
